title: Player fixation upgrades incidental set dressing into an invitational, then the DM releases control
prep_expectation: Victor/Frankenstein exists in the Highgate material as background texture attached to the Big Sleep office; the rough draft does not lay out a Victor adventure or required confrontation.

prep_sources.note: Highgate lists the Big Sleep, Frankenstein/Franklin S. Tyne, a suspicious helper, and Igor as location material rather than a scripted adventure.

live_timeline.channel: 🛣 Week one, The Red Road / highgate-cemetery
live_timeline.event: When players propose waking Victor's creation, Brendon recognizes that as enough new scope to require a second invitational rather than improvising unlimited infrastructure on the spot.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (that sounds like an invitational part 2. I'd need to set up other things)

live_timeline.brendon_text: (no. I am taking my hands off the wheel. words didn't work)

live_timeline.channel: 🛣 Week one, The Red Road / highgate-cemetery
live_timeline.event: He makes the physical situation clear and gives the players control of what happens to Victor.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (mausoleum. solid stone. the part left when victor yelled get out. you have an empty building to do what you want with this characer. the agency is yours)

live_timeline.channel: 🛣 Week one, The Red Road / highgate-cemetery
live_timeline.event: When players themselves conflict over Victor, he offers either formal turn-order/contested resolution or listening to one another, rather than choosing their desired outcome.
live_timeline.brendon_text: Yes their is rope. Yes you are alone. In case you hadn't noticed. He isn't resisting you. You have competing parties trying to have agency. We can either go into turn order and roll against one anther for things like deception and persuasion. Or you guys can actually listen to one another instead of just talking over one another in a scramble.

signal_noticed: Repeated player attention transformed a minor background element into a meaningful shared concern: research, letters, conversation, and concrete plans kept returning to Victor.
adaptation: Promote the incidental NPC into a deliberately scoped invitational, connect it to existing fiction, and prepare enough to make the pursuit real. Once the scene becomes a genuine player moral conflict, stop steering the outcome.
downstream_change: A location detail that was not intended to be explorable became a multi-day player-driven story. The DM supplied access and consequences but did not require the confrontation to resolve according to a prewritten Victor plot.
rejected_alternatives: Tell players Victor is background-only and close the thread.
Expand every new idea immediately without regard to prep scope.
Use Victor or the NPC crowd to force the players toward the DM's preferred moral resolution.
decision_rule: IF players repeatedly invest in an incidental element, THEN promote it into playable content when it can support a real story; scope new preparation honestly, and once the promoted story belongs to the players, do not pre-solve its outcome.
caveats: The rough draft proves Victor was lightly sketched, while Brendon's live statement explicitly confirms he was not originally intended to be explorable.

title: Combat presentation is treated as an interface to iterate, not a sacred procedure
prep_expectation: Roanoke explicitly aims to combine tabletop improvisation with the functionality and user interface of video games. The Grey Render event supplies a concrete combat situation but does not prescribe the Discord interaction format.

prep_sources.note: High-level experience goal: persistent RP environment combining TTRPG improvisation with video-game functionality/UI.
Grey Render event supplies the encounter content; the live format remains open.

I will be running a highly experimental event that will be hybrid -text and voice. I will be experimenting with form and function to attempt to help speed up combat. And you will be experimenting with Dr. Willemina Render in an adventure I call. Billy 2: Billie. 6pm PST tonight.)

The entire adventure will be using a single init, both for exploration and combat. In addition, you will be broken into teams of three. Keep meta discussions to OOC. On your teams turn you all act at once. There are a few other things, I'm going to try too. On your team's turn I will respond to the act...

live_timeline.brendon_text: The way distance works is this: You are either at melee, ranged, or distant. movement cost is 15 feet between them. Please state your distance as the first part of your answer.

live_timeline.event: The next day he reuses the movement abstraction, showing that useful pieces survive the experiment.

live_timeline.event: For the Week 1 final event he changes the spatial/UI scheme again—text rooms and quadrants represent position—and explicitly says he has heard complaints and they are still innovating.
live_timeline.brendon_text: Preregister your initiative here.  Groups will be divided between rooms by init. Range will be divided by text chat. I will move between rooms to ensure everyone gets resolved. Moving between text rooms represents using 15 feet of vertical  movement (on a top down map, north to south). The map will be divide by left and right to represent horizontal movement. Each quadrant represents a 15 foot square. Moving between voice channels will not be permitted except on your turn for communication. M...

signal_noticed: Combat speed and Discord legibility were themselves part of the play experience; the first implementation generated enough friction to merit redesign.
adaptation: Experiment in public, keep pieces that help, revise pieces that do not, and redesign the interface around the next event's needs rather than defending the previous procedure.
downstream_change: Movement abstraction persists, while the larger event adopts a different channel/quadrant structure. Player complaints become design input rather than evidence that experimentation should stop.
rejected_alternatives: Run standard tabletop combat unchanged despite Discord friction.
Treat the first experimental format as a permanent rule because players already learned it.
Abandon experimentation after complaints.
decision_rule: IF the medium makes otherwise-good play slow or illegible, THEN treat presentation and procedure as adjustable DM tools: test, observe, preserve useful parts, and revise the rest.
caveats: This case teaches process judgment about running the game, not a preference for these exact 2020 Discord mechanics.

title: A request to erase painful memory becomes a persistent character motif instead of a reset button
prep_expectation: Golden Dawn is prepared as a secretive apocalyptic faction built around sacrifice, misread prophecy, and betrayal. Its through-line is meant to emerge in pieces through interaction.

prep_sources.note: Through-lines are delivered in pieces; Golden Dawn is structured around sacrifice, secrecy, and betrayal.
The planned faction has a multi-week arc with sabotage and later revelations.

live_timeline.event: A player asks for their character to forget the Golden Dawn entirely after a faction crisis.
Another player asks whether the missing spellcasting requirement should simply be handwaved.
Brendon refuses to handwave because he recognizes the question as a good character arc.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (thats an interesting question. I won't hand wave. this is good arc)

live_timeline.event: He narrows the memory alteration: forget the trial, retain allegiance; leaving the faction still requires a new character reason.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (modify memory, the trial is forgotten, but not their allegiance. If you still want to leave after, rp another reason)

live_timeline.event: He explicitly preserves the player's ability to choose their story.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (and player agency. they can choose their story)

live_timeline.event: He implements sleep, modify memory, and a magic-mouth effect rather than erasing all traces.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (sleep, modify memory, and magic mouth on web)

live_timeline.event: The new persistent motif is defined: before Golden Dawn violence, the character hears 'look away.'
live_timeline.brendon_text: (any time your character is about to see violence done by the golden dawn it will whisper "look away")

live_timeline.event: The motif is actually triggered the next day, proving it is carried forward rather than being flavor stated once.
live_timeline.brendon_text: "Look away web."

live_timeline.event: The motif recurs during another violent situation.
live_timeline.brendon_text: "Look away web. Please Look away."

live_timeline.channel: 🚢 Week two, The Tir Na Nog / 🥐-the-mess-hall
live_timeline.event: The player incorporates the effect into character conversation, making it part of the character's self-understanding.
The player later folds the memory alteration and 'look away' motif into nightmares and identity concerns.
Near the end of the season Brendon checks whether the character remembers the original trial.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (you remembered the trial of rah?)

live_timeline.event: The player gives a long retrospective in which the faction, memory manipulation, and choice to look away remain central to the character's accumulated history.

signal_noticed: The request was mechanically simple but narratively expensive: fully erasing the faction would also erase allegiance, responsibility, betrayal, and future identity choices.
adaptation: Grant a narrower form of the requested change while creating a recurring sensory handle that keeps the consequence playable.
downstream_change: A one-scene request becomes a motif that recurs for weeks and is eventually used by the player as part of the character's own account of who they became.
rejected_alternatives: Handwave total amnesia and remove the problem from play.
Deny the request outright merely to preserve the faction plot.
Treat the memory change as a one-time cosmetic event with no later consequences.
decision_rule: IF a requested shortcut would erase a choice-bearing character problem, THEN preserve the player's intended relief while retaining a smaller persistent consequence that can generate future play.
caveats: This is strong evidence of how Brendon protects story-bearing consequences; it should not be generalized into always adding trauma or magical complications.

title: A danger that lands unfairly produces a telegraphing correction that changes later delivery
prep_expectation: The campaign is supposed to include horrific encounters and escalating pressure that turns survivors into capable adventurers; the rough draft contains numerous dangerous events but does not itself establish how clearly danger should be signaled.

prep_sources.note: The intended experience includes overcoming horrific encounters inside a persistent character-centered game.

live_timeline.event: During a table-trust discussion Brendon explains that pressure on the ship and at home was meant to turn survivors into capable adventuring parties.
live_timeline.brendon_text: The pressure of the ship and now the haven of your home are meant to turn you from survivors to capable adventuring parties. It was never my intention to cause Web or Baeshra harm.

live_timeline.event: He identifies his own delivery failure: he should have signaled the deadliness better through roleplay.
live_timeline.brendon_text: And I know I should have signaled better how deadly through rp.

live_timeline.event: He commits to transparency with the players.
live_timeline.brendon_text: I will always be transparant with you.

live_timeline.event: He cancels that night's event rather than pushing through a damaged table state.
live_timeline.brendon_text: I'm canceling tonight's event.

live_timeline.event: Eight days later, before a deadly Lake of Woes encounter, he directly warns players that what is ahead is deadly and tells them to play safe and smart.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (what is coming up is a deadly encounter. Play safe. Play smart. Don't freeze up and do nothing. Rp is great, but I want you to live.)

signal_noticed: The desired challenge had produced the wrong experience because players lacked enough information to understand the risk before committing.
adaptation: Own the communication error, stop escalation while trust is strained, and later change how lethal stakes are telegraphed.
downstream_change: The campaign remains dangerous, but later danger is made legible before the players commit to it.
rejected_alternatives: Conclude that lethal challenge itself was the mistake and remove danger.
Defend the original scene because the rules allowed the consequence.
Continue the scheduled event despite a damaged table state.
decision_rule: IF a consequence is mechanically legitimate but lands as unfair because the risk was not legible, THEN fix the telegraphing and table state before changing the underlying danger.
caveats: Private player disclosures surrounding the August 4 discussion are deliberately omitted; the evidence used here is Brendon's own diagnosis and later changed behavior.

title: Players choose an objective through a live war; unchosen fronts continue moving without them
prep_expectation: After the hags are defeated, the rough draft calls for a long-running conflict between the Uru and Chinnokin, with both sides initially hostile. Later calendar beats keep that conflict active.

prep_sources.note: The Uru/Chinnokin conflict is a prepared persistent pressure, not a single encounter.
Week 3-4 calendar continues Chinnokin, war, lake, and later threat beats.

live_timeline.event: Brendon identifies three materially different routes: fight toward Longshadow, fight toward the Fishmother, or cross the battlefield to pursue the temple objective; players must choose.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (You have 3 choices in my mind. Elevator fight to talk to longshadow, fight the sea fury to talk to the fishmother, or attempt to cross the battlefield and then run the temple adventure. You need to choose and dm me.)

live_timeline.event: On arrival the war is already in motion, with both leaders advancing through active siege warfare.
live_timeline.brendon_text: When you arrive there is Chaos all around. Siege machines, both aerial and water based are laying waste to droves of soldiers on either side. There is some scattered fighting near you (on the eastern edge of the map) but no one has yet taken an interest in you. The Fishmother and longshadow are wading through the fray slowly making their way toward one another. Fireballs and lightning bolts are ripping through the battle field windwalls and water walls are making what amounts to be trench war...

live_timeline.event: While the party pursues its route, Longshadow notices them.
live_timeline.brendon_text: Longshadow notices the group

live_timeline.event: Longshadow attacks the group with lightning, creating a relationship consequence without forcing the party to switch objectives.
live_timeline.brendon_text: he casts lightning bolt on the group (if there is any arguments about positioning I can always change it to chain lightning)

live_timeline.event: Later that night Brendon announces that Longshadow is dead and Empty Hill's usurpation has succeeded while the players were engaged elsewhere.
live_timeline.brendon_text: @everyone Longshadow is dead. Long may the Chinnokin reign. Empty Hill's plan to usurp power over roostloft has succeeded.

live_timeline.event: A player summarizes that Longshadow attacked them on sight and they consequently chose not to befriend him.
A player-authored town bulletin integrates both the temple result and the political consequences of Longshadow's replacement.
More than a week later, the group sees devastation at Roostloft and Brendon ties it directly to the Uru defeat at Lake of Woes.
live_timeline.brendon_text: Rockman, as a machine of war, it is clear to you that this is the result of their defeat in the battle of lake of the woes.

live_timeline.event: An Uru survivor now seeks the party's help demonstrating peaceful coexistence, turning the old war outcome into a new social situation.
live_timeline.brendon_text: "Roanoke. I'd knew you would come. Do not be afraid. I'm here to help to you, yes. Come, show them Roanokes live with Uru together in peace. Please.."

signal_noticed: The players chose a goal that crossed an active conflict instead of choosing one faction's story. Their route still exposed them to faction behavior while the rest of the war had its own momentum.
adaptation: Let the party cross the conflict toward its chosen objective, allow NPC factions to act on them when appropriate, and resolve the unchosen front independently.
downstream_change: The players never needed to formally 'pick a side' for the war to matter. The offscreen result changed leadership, settlement condition, and later opportunities for reconciliation.
rejected_alternatives: Freeze the war until players choose a faction.
Require the party to complete a faction encounter before allowing the temple objective.
Treat the offscreen war as irrelevant because the players did not directly participate in its climax.
decision_rule: IF players pursue an objective through a larger active conflict, THEN preserve their chosen objective while simulating the other fronts; let route, exposure, and NPC action create consequences without requiring explicit faction allegiance.
caveats: This case shows persistent-world handling of simultaneous fronts, not a requirement to resolve every unattended conflict offscreen.

title: A fully authored final week is deliberately decompressed so accumulated player history can drive play
prep_expectation: The rough draft contains a day-by-day Week 5 spine: Aether ritual, meteor/spelljammer, Ossuary, Tinker story, Tinker return, infernal well, and Hunger finale.

prep_sources.note: Week 5 is strongly pre-authored in the rough draft.

live_timeline.event: Before Week 5, Brendon asks the group to DM him the things they still wish to explore or accomplish.
live_timeline.brendon_text: What I need from the group going forward is dms about things you wish to explore or accomplish

live_timeline.event: He states that Week 5 is deliberately far less written so players can lead and DMs can accommodate more invitationals.
live_timeline.brendon_text: The game is far less written in week 5 to let the players lead more and the dms to be able to accommodate more invitationals

live_timeline.event: He tells the whole server that the next week will be much more player-led while preserving some major prepared fights.
live_timeline.brendon_text: @everyone Hell week is almost over. You have done well to make it this far. Next week will be a lot more player led, (I mean, I still have some very bdfm and noah fights planned for you all, but it should be a bit less intense.) Band together. And prepare all that you can for the final fight. It will be the most epic battle we have ever put before you in Roanoke. Tonight and Tomorrow will be rough, but I know you can get through it.

live_timeline.event: During Week 5 he announces a short window in which he can run something.
live_timeline.brendon_text: I have an hour and a half to run something

live_timeline.event: Instead of supplying a fixed encounter, he gives players a deadline to organize and choose what they want to pursue.
live_timeline.brendon_text: I'll give it to 4:40 for you all to get organized and pick something, any later than that and even an rp session wont have enough time

live_timeline.event: He explicitly frames the resulting scene as the players' invitational.
live_timeline.brendon_text: this is their invitational

live_timeline.event: At the start of the scene he asks the players what they would like to do rather than revealing a preselected mission.
live_timeline.brendon_text: What would you like to do?

signal_noticed: After four weeks, the campaign had accumulated enough unfinished goals, relationships, faction business, and player priorities that speculative fixed prep was less valuable than reserved response capacity.
adaptation: Keep anchor events and major fights, but intentionally remove density between them and solicit unresolved player priorities as the source for invitationals.
downstream_change: Week 5 becomes a hybrid: prepared finale architecture plus player-selected scenes generated from the history of actual play.
rejected_alternatives: Run every prepared day in order because it exists in the document.
Discard the finale spine entirely in favor of pure improvisation.
Wait for players to stumble into unresolved business without actively soliciting priorities.
decision_rule: IF campaign history has become richer than speculative prep, THEN keep only the anchor beats that still matter and convert remaining prep bandwidth into responses to unresolved player priorities.
caveats: The rough draft and live statements conflict in authored density by design; the live statements explicitly establish that the reduction was intentional.

title: When campaign architecture produces the wrong social game, rewrite the architecture and audit its dependent mechanics
prep_expectation: Season 3 is designed around four organizations with distinct motives and week-by-week faction arcs, including separate endgame functions.

prep_sources.note: Four organizations are a structural premise of the campaign.
Factions have separate weekly progression and ending logic.

live_timeline.event: Brendon states that the season's focus is bringing the players together as friends/family rather than through governance.
live_timeline.brendon_text: and this years focus has been about bringing you all together not through governance, but by you all coming together as friends and family.

live_timeline.event: He says the last week is about coming back together and identifies renewed player blame/toxicity as a risk.
live_timeline.brendon_text: The last week is about coming back together. Blame throwing for players might bring back some of the Toxicity from previous weeks that we have been trying to calm.

live_timeline.event: He diagnoses that a mayoral race turned the game into a bipartisan all-or-nothing structure even though the Mason story was meant to concern something else.
live_timeline.brendon_text: The masons were designed to be further away from politics anyways. I put copper in the running because he is a capable and wise player. But I set the cornerstone on the pub, because our story was meant to be about something other than governance. But the mayoral race became bipartisan. And bipartisanship is allways all or nothing.

live_timeline.event: He acknowledges causing immediate drama while trying to contain the larger drama created by bipartisanship.
live_timeline.brendon_text: I get that I just caused drama, but I promise its because I'm terrified of the drama that already happened from bipartisanship that your spreading

live_timeline.event: He publicly names the broken design assumption: four active factions collapsed to two after two DMs became less active. He and Noah eliminate the winner-take-all bipartisan ending and redefine Masons as defense/barrier restoration and Knights as offense/binding-killing the Hunger.
live_timeline.brendon_text: @everyone When we designed this game it was intended to have 4 active factions. 4 separate stories, each with their own separate quests to work toward influencing the ending. Through no fault of their own two of the DMs had to become less active. This left us with a Bi-Partisan system winner take all scenario. Its toxic and has been the source of much of the drama that we have had to address. Noah and I are making the choice to eliminate the bipartisan aspect of the game. The mason ending is ...

live_timeline.event: He then audits downstream mechanics and removes the planned 'destroy your tools mid-combat to poison the Hunger' mechanic because it no longer makes sense after the ending rewrite.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (So my retcon for lore, to keep the peace, that the souls from the soulforge will become a barrier after the game. Which means that mechanic by which I was planning on have you destroy the tools mid combat to poison the hunger making the sacrifice feel more meaningful after all the work you put on them might not be nessisary. I'm rethinking the issue, but for now, lets just go ahead and strike the "destroy your tools during the fight" mechanic because it no longer makes sense.)

live_timeline.event: The following day the revised fiction supports cooperation and division of responsibility instead of faction exclusivity.
live_timeline.brendon_text: "Right. Well, then I suppose I'll leave it to you to organize the family. Your plan is a good one. And it looks like this emergency is well in hand. Between you and the Archivist and the other masons, I think we have a good balance."

signal_noticed: A structural assumption in prep failed in production: four active faction lanes collapsed into a two-sided winner-take-all political game that was undermining the intended social experience.
adaptation: Change the ending architecture itself, explain the causal reason, preserve distinct faction contributions without exclusivity, then remove mechanics whose meaning depended on the old architecture.
downstream_change: The finale can now answer the campaign's recurring 'can the town work together?' question with an in-world yes. The rewrite propagates through lore and mechanics rather than existing as a cosmetic retcon.
rejected_alternatives: Preserve the original faction competition because it was prewritten.
Solve only the social argument while leaving the same winner-take-all endgame incentives intact.
Retcon the ending but leave obsolete mechanics in place.
decision_rule: IF a campaign-level design assumption fails and begins producing an experience contrary to the campaign's central purpose, THEN rewrite the architecture at the level where the failure originates and audit every dependent rule, reward, and scene for coherence.
caveats: This is one of the strongest architecture-level cases in the corpus because Brendon explicitly states both the original assumption and why it failed.

title: A preplanned boss-sized fight is replaced with a smaller responsive encounter that preserves what players actually want
prep_expectation: The final week contains large authored set pieces and a climactic Hunger sequence. Late-week prepared combat therefore exists inside an already dense finale structure.

prep_sources.note: The final week contains major ritual, spelljammer, infernal, and Hunger combat material.

live_timeline.event: He immediately conditions that option on whether it would actually be satisfying.

live_timeline.brendon_text: otherwise, I can throw mobs instead of bosses, but it will be too long for vee

live_timeline.event: Because the party is small, he avoids formal initiative and resolves the encounter fluidly.
live_timeline.brendon_text: (no init called yet, small party, will resolve as we go.)

live_timeline.event: During the resulting emergent scene he remarks that this is the movie he wants to watch.
live_timeline.brendon_text: this is the movie I want to watch

live_timeline.event: The replacement route naturally reaches Roostloft and reveals the lasting consequence of the earlier Lake of Woes war.
live_timeline.brendon_text: Rockman, as a machine of war, it is clear to you that this is the result of their defeat in the battle of lake of the woes.

signal_noticed: The prepared encounter no longer matched party size, resources, available time, or the activity mix the players still wanted.
adaptation: Do not merely delete combat. Scale the activity to current constraints, keep some danger because players want it, simplify resolution, and attach the replacement to an existing player-led route.
downstream_change: The party gets satisfying play without a compromised boss fight, and the substitute encounter carries them into consequential existing fiction.
rejected_alternatives: Run the boss encounter as written despite depleted resources.
Remove combat entirely even though players wanted some.
Scale the boss down mechanically while preserving an encounter structure too large for the available time.
decision_rule: IF a prepared encounter no longer fits the table, THEN identify the experience players still want, deliver the smallest encounter that honestly supplies it, and use that replacement to advance existing fiction.
caveats: The exact identity of the skipped preplanned fight is not required for this judgment and is not inferred here.

title: A table boundary stated after friction becomes a hard gate in later adjudication
prep_expectation: The rough draft defines a persistent, RP-heavy environment centered on characters' daily lives and group continuity, but it does not specify the later PvP consent rule. The strongest source here is therefore live policy followed by later live enforcement.

prep_sources.note: General persistent-RP/group-centered baseline only; no exact PvP rule is claimed from prep.

live_timeline.event: Brendon restates a clear rule: PvP requires a DM and consent from both players.
live_timeline.brendon_text: ok. So. There is a clear rule that I'd like to restate. The rule is that there is no PVP with out a dm. That means with out a DM's consent. If there is a fight that is to be resolved between two parties by combat, that is something that we accommodate. But not with out consent from both players and a dm.

live_timeline.event: He broadens the point beyond combat, stating that pressuring other players to play in ways they do not want is unacceptable.
live_timeline.brendon_text: Additionally. I'm a little disappointed that players were pressuring other players to play in a way that they didn't want to. I understand the joy of trying to get others to come play. But consent is more than just a consideration. No means no.

live_timeline.brendon_text: (I have to obey player agency. PvP was not granted for anything other than casting. I can't roll to let you stop him. No rolls to stop him, but following is not pvp.)

live_timeline.brendon_text: (Does anyone have any objections to my ruling or are feeling that this matter was handled unfairly? I can ask another DM to adjudicate and recluse myself if I need to. But I need a game where you trust your dm, after week one, I am not willing to move forward with out consent. If so dm me at this time.)

signal_noticed: A previous table conflict had shown that ordinary simulation logic is not enough to adjudicate player-versus-player interference safely or fairly.
adaptation: Turn consent into a gate that determines which actions are eligible for mechanical resolution at all. Permit adjacent non-PvP actions without broadening the granted consent.
downstream_change: The later scene is adjudicated according to the boundary established days earlier, even though a normal contested roll could have simulated the attempted interference.
rejected_alternatives: Treat PvP consent as merely a modifier or preference and roll anyway.
Assume consent to one hostile action covers the whole confrontation.
Ban every adjacent action once PvP is constrained.
decision_rule: IF the table has established a consent boundary, THEN treat it as an eligibility condition for adjudication rather than another fact inside the simulation; resolve only the scope actually consented to.
caveats: This is a live-policy longitudinal case rather than a prep-versus-play case. It belongs because it demonstrates that once Brendon makes a table-level rule, he later subordinates simulation to it.
